title: Unix timestamps: 10-digit seconds vs 13-digit milliseconds, 2038
description: Tell 10-digit seconds from 13-digit milliseconds: where each range ends, why time zones only affect display, and how to check and convert a suspect value.
content:
A Unix timestamp is an absolute instant measured from 1970-01-01 UTC. Ten digits usually mean seconds and 13 digits mean milliseconds — three digits apart. When you are tracking down a time that landed in the wrong place, confirm the unit first and look at the time zone second, because the time zone only affects display.

Seconds and milliseconds: one scale, two precisions

A timestamp records only how many units have passed since the origin; whether the unit is a second or a millisecond is fixed by the protocol, and the number itself carries no unit information. The same instant can be written as 1794787200 or as 1794787200000, and both point at 2026-11-16T00:00:00Z.

The difference is resolution alone: second precision compresses every change within a second into one number, while millisecond precision keeps thousandths. The factor is always 1000, so 13 digits and 10 digits differ by exactly three places — which is where the “count the digits, guess the unit” rule of thumb comes from.

DigitsUsual unitThe same instant asResolvable
10 digitsSeconds17947872001 second
13 digitsMilliseconds17947872000001 millisecond
16 digitsMicroseconds17947872000000001 microsecond
19 digitsNanoseconds17947872000000000001 nanosecond

But the digit count is a clue, not a protocol. An 11- or 12-digit value may be a millisecond reading from before 2001, or a time value that someone rescaled; 14 digits are still in millisecond territory (13-digit milliseconds last until 2286, and only after that do 14 digits appear naturally), and only 16 digits mean microseconds, 19 nanoseconds. The reliable evidence is the API documentation, the field name, and one sanity check against a known value.

Why it is 10 digits and 13 digits today

Seconds crossed into 10 digits on 2001-09-09: 1000000000 is 2001-09-09T01:46:40Z. Milliseconds crossed into 13 digits on almost the same day: 1000000000000 is also 2001-09-09T01:46:40Z. Both rulers grew at the same moment, which is why what you see today is 10 digits and 13 digits.

The end of each range is equally tidy: the largest 10-digit second value is 9999999999, which is 2286-11-20T17:46:39Z, and the largest 13-digit millisecond value is 9999999999999, which is 2286-11-20T17:46:39.999Z. That is simply where the decimal digits run out, not a cut-off defined by any standard.

Equating 10 digits with a “32-bit integer” is a common misunderstanding. Ten decimal digits reach into the billions, while a signed 32-bit integer stops at 2147483647. The two “bits” are not the same thing at all: one is ten decimal digits, the other is thirty-two binary bits.

The 2038 problem applies only to signed 32-bit seconds

2147483647 seconds is 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z. Add one second and you get 2147483648, which in a 64-bit environment still prints correctly as 2038-01-19T03:14:08Z; but on a system that stores only int32 it wraps around to -2147483648, that is 1901-12-13T20:45:52Z. That is the whole of the 2038 problem: the fault is in the storage width, not in the timestamp format.

The same constant applied to milliseconds is a completely different story: 2147483647 milliseconds is only 1970-01-25T20:31:23.647Z, barely three weeks past the epoch. So “32-bit overflow” has to be stated together with the unit, or you will reach the opposite conclusion.

  • A second-based int32 field: overflows in 2038, the most typical migration target.
  • A millisecond-based int32 field: already overflowed in January 1970 and rarely seen in practice; seeing one is a reason to suspect a wrong unit first.
  • 64-bit seconds: about 292.28 billion years (2922.8 × 10^8 years), nothing to worry about in engineering terms.
  • At the moment of 2038 the millisecond value is 2147483648000, still within 13 digits and unrelated to 32 bits.

A timestamp is an absolute UTC instant; TZ only changes display

The same 1794787200 shows as 2026-11-16 00:00:00 in UTC, 2026-11-16 08:00:00 in Asia/Shanghai and 2026-11-15 19:00:00 in America/New_York. The number has not changed; only the time zone used for formatting has.

A form with an offset expresses the same instant too: 2026-11-16T08:00:00+08:00 and 2026-11-16T00:00:00Z parse to equal time values. What really deserves caution is mistaking a “display difference” for a “data difference” and going on to change the value in the database — that is what produces a genuine shift.

Servers on UTC and browsers on local time is a normal deployment: the API passes a number, the page renders it in the local time zone. Conversely, if the API passes a string with no offset, each receiver parses it in its own time zone and you really do end up hours apart.

The offset itself moves as well: America/New_York is -05:00 in November and -04:00 in summer, while Asia/Shanghai is +08:00 all year with no daylight saving. Use a fixed +8 to reason about another region and you will be an hour out sooner or later.

The screenshot was captured in a UTC environment: the tool shows “Local time” according to the time zone of the environment it runs in, which is why in UTC that row and the “ISO time” row carry the same value; switch the time zone to +08:00 and convert again, and the first row becomes 08:00:00.

Parsing traps: date-only versus date-time strings

ECMAScript specifies that a string holding only a date is parsed as UTC, while a string with a time but no offset is parsed as local time. Run the two lines below on a machine at +08:00 and the results differ by 8 hours.

new Date('2024-01-01')        // 2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z, prints 08:00 in local time
new Date('2024-01-01T00:00')  // 2023-12-31T16:00:00.000Z, prints 00:00 in local time

The literals differ by a few characters, yet the meaning moves from “UTC midnight” to “local midnight”. When you hand time between systems, send an ISO 8601 string with an offset, or send a timestamp directly; do not send a date-time string without an offset and leave the other side to guess.

For the same reason, how Date.parse handles non-standard formats depends on the implementation, and the same text can come out differently in Node and in a browser. If you need stability, use standard formats only, or validate the format once before parsing.

Three steps to identify the unit

  1. Record the raw value and the field name; do not keep only the formatted date, or the evidence is lost on the spot.
  2. Screen by digit count: 10 digits means seconds and 13 digits means milliseconds; 11 and 12 digits cannot be guessed and must be checked against the documentation.
  3. Work back from a known value: 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z should be 1704067200; if you get 1704067200000, the unit is milliseconds.
Date.now()                      // 1794787200123, milliseconds, 13 digits
Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)   // 1794787200, truncates milliseconds into seconds
import time, datetime
time.time()        # seconds, float, with a fraction
time.time_ns()     # nanosecond integer, 19 digits
datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(1794787200)     # in the local time zone
datetime.datetime.utcfromtimestamp(1794787200)  # in UTC

The same second prints as two different clock readings in Python: 2026-11-16 08:00:00 locally and 2026-11-16 00:00:00 in UTC. That is not a precision problem but the display difference caused by a different time zone argument.

Default units across languages and APIs

The easiest trap while debugging is assuming that every runtime uses the same unit. The “Unit” column in the table below records the default behaviour confirmed by each runtime's documentation and by direct testing; the “Example value” column uses the same fixed instant, 2026-11-16T00:00:00Z (with 123 added on the millisecond row), so the rows can be compared side by side — these are not live readings from any particular machine.

CallUnitExample value (fixed instant 2026-11-16T00:00:00Z)
Date.now() (browser and Node)Milliseconds1794787200123
process.hrtime.bigint() (Node)Nanoseconds, monotonic clockNot a Unix time: the reference point is an arbitrary moment (the Node documentation calls it an arbitrary time in the past), used only to measure intervals
time.time() (Python)Seconds, float1794787200 (float, actually prints with a fraction)
time.time_ns() (Python)Nanoseconds1794787200000000000
datetime.fromtimestamp() (Python)Seconds, in the local time zone2026-11-16 08:00:00
datetime.utcfromtimestamp() (Python)Seconds, in UTC2026-11-16 00:00:00

Symptom cheat sheet for common API mistakes

SymptomUsual causeOne-step check
The time lands in January 1970Seconds treated as milliseconds1794787200 shows up as 1970-01-21T18:33:07.200Z
The date runs tens of thousands of years into the futureMilliseconds treated as seconds1794787200000 shows up as the year 58844 AD
Everything is off by whole hours (8 hours at +08:00)The rendering time zone differs; the value itself is correctPrint the UTC result and the business-zone result side by side
The date is one day early or one day lateA string with no offset parsed as UTCSwitch to an ISO 8601 string with an offset
The last digits are flattened (9007199254740993 reads as 9007199254740992)Beyond Number's safe integerUse BigInt, or carry the value as a string end to end

Precision ladder: milliseconds, microseconds, nanoseconds

Date.now only goes down to milliseconds, yet performance.timeOrigin carries a fraction, which shows that the underlying clock is finer than a millisecond and Date simply truncates it when it builds the value. Measure elapsed time with a monotonic clock rather than a wall clock, or a single system time correction can turn the difference negative.

Nanosecond integers already exceed the range Number can represent exactly. 9007199254740991 is the largest integer JavaScript represents exactly, 16 digits in all; write 9007199254740993 into it and it reads back as 9007199254740992, the last digit simply gone. A nanosecond timestamp is 19 digits and must be carried as a BigInt or a string.

Conversely, milliseconds are enough for ordinary business time: 13-digit milliseconds do not run out of digits until 2286, and the precision already separates most human actions.

Batch and boundaries: negative values, leap seconds, safe integers

  • Negative values are valid: -1 is 1969-12-31T23:59:59Z and -86400 is 1969-12-31T00:00:00Z. Birthdays and historical records from before 1970 will all come out negative.
  • There are no leap seconds: Unix time fixes every day at 86400 seconds, so 1970-01-01 to 2024-01-01 is 19723 days and 1704067200 seconds. Where you need to align with TAI, convert separately.
  • The representation has a ceiling: the ECMAScript time value tops out at 8640000000000000 milliseconds, which is +275760-09-13; one more and it is Invalid Date.

Storage and transport: field names beat comments

Do not leave the unit to a comment. Naming the field expires_at_seconds or created_at_ms, or declaring it a 64-bit integer in the API definition with the unit noted, saves the next person one bad afternoon.

Across languages, a string is steadier than a number: 13-digit milliseconds fit in a 64-bit integer in most languages, but once they pass through JavaScript's Number there is the 2^53 ceiling, and nanoseconds will certainly be truncated.

Databases commonly offer two ways to store it as well: an integer timestamp, or a native date-time type. The first has no time zone semantics and compares easily, but you have to check whether it holds seconds or milliseconds; the second carries time zone semantics, but the default time zone behaviour is not consistent across databases. Picking one and writing it down is safer than mixing the two.

Readability and machine processing can be split: use ISO 8601 with an offset for display and logs, and integer timestamps for computation and storage. RFC 3339 defines the former, and it can express the offset; two such strings can be compared directly as text only when their offsets and their fractional digits also match.

Boundaries and limits

This article and the accompanying tool can answer three questions: does this number look like a timestamp, is it seconds or milliseconds, and what does it display as in a given time zone. They cannot decide the business meaning for you.

  • The digit heuristic is just that: the tool reads 11 and 12 digits as milliseconds, so 17040672000 becomes 1970-07-17 and 100000000000 becomes 1973-03-03, and the interface never warns that the digit count looks suspicious.
  • The tool accepts only 10–13 plain digits: 9 digits, negative numbers, 14 digits or more, and input containing letters all get the same message, “Please enter a 10-digit (seconds) or 13-digit (milliseconds) numeric timestamp.”
  • A failed conversion does not clear the result box: the previous successful output stays where it was, so a misread hands you a stale result — check the status line before you conclude anything.
  • Display follows the browser's local time zone and the page has no switch for the time zone; to compare another zone, use the World Clock.
  • Leap seconds, microseconds and nanoseconds are not supported; 13-digit milliseconds is the upper bound it handles.
  • A timestamp marks an instant, not a business day. Daily reports, accounting periods and cut-off times that cross time zones need an extra business-zone convention, and that part cannot be solved by conversion.

Check your judgement in the tool

Open the Timestamp Converter page, paste the suspect number into the input box and convert: first check whether the “Unit” row says seconds or milliseconds, then compare the “Local time” and “ISO time” rows — the first moves with the time zone, the second is always UTC. At +08:00 an 8-hour gap between them means the problem is in display, while an absurd year means the problem is in the unit.

To line time up across time zones, use the World Clock to watch several cities at once; to work out how many days lie between two dates rather than how many milliseconds between two instants, use the Date Difference Calculator. Keeping “instant” and “calendar day” apart saves about half of all time zone tickets.

faqs.q: Can 10-digit and 13-digit timestamps be converted into each other directly?
faqs.a: Yes. Divide the 13-digit millisecond value by 1000 and round down to get the 10-digit second value, and multiply by 1000 the other way; the conversion drops the millisecond fraction.

faqs.q: Why does the same timestamp show a different date on two machines?
faqs.a: A timestamp denotes one instant, and the displayed result depends on the time zone used when formatting it. Print UTC and local time side by side and you can confirm that the difference comes from display, not from the data.

faqs.q: Will the 2038 problem break 13-digit millisecond timestamps?
faqs.a: No. The 2038 problem concerns seconds stored in a signed 32-bit integer; at that moment the 13-digit millisecond value is 2147483648000, which has nothing to do with a 32-bit width.

faqs.q: What unit is an 11- or 12-digit number?
faqs.a: The digit count alone cannot tell. It may be a millisecond reading from an early date, or a second value that has been rescaled; you have to check the API documentation, or work back from a known value to verify it.
